subject: Civil Engineering
title: Soil Amplification
description: Learn Soil Amplification in one minute.

hook.text: The 1985 Mexico City earthquake killed 10,000 — but the epicenter was 200 miles away.

buildup.text: Mexico City sits on an ancient lakebed. Soft clay amplified seismic waves dramatically.

discovery.text: Soft soil vibrates at lower frequencies — matching the natural sway of mid-rise buildings.

twist.text: Buildings on soft soil experienced shaking ten times stronger than buildings on nearby rock.

climax.text: Seismic site classification maps soil type — Site Class A (rock) to E (soft clay).

punchline.text: The same earthquake shakes soft soil ten times harder than rock. Location is everything.

quiz.question: Why were buildings in Mexico City so heavily damaged in 1985 despite the distant epicenter?
options: Buildings were constructed with weaker materials than surrounding cities
Soft lakebed soil amplified seismic waves, increasing shaking intensity dramatically
The earthquake triggered a secondary fault directly beneath the city

details.summary: Soft soil deposits amplify earthquake ground motion as seismic waves slow down and increase in amplitude when they travel from hard rock into softer overlying soils. Lake beds, river deltas, and artificial fill can amplify shaking by 2 to 10 times compared to nearby rock sites.
details.whyItMatters: Soil amplification explains why earthquake damage is often concentrated in areas with soft soil, such as Mexico City, the San Francisco Marina District, and Christchurch, rather than distributed uniformly.
takeaways: Seismic waves slow down in soft soil, increasing amplitude to conserve energy
Soft clay and fill deposits can amplify shaking 2 to 10 times relative to rock
Building codes require site classification to account for soil amplification

faq.question: Why do soft soils amplify earthquake ground motion?
faq.answer: Seismic waves travel faster in hard rock and slow down in soft soil. To conserve energy as velocity decreases, wave amplitude must increase. Additionally, soft soil layers can trap and resonate with seismic waves at their natural frequency, further amplifying specific periods of motion.

faq.question: How do building codes account for soil amplification effects?
faq.answer: Codes classify sites into categories from hard rock to soft clay based on soil properties measured to 30 meters depth. Each category has amplification factors that increase the design ground motion.
